description_ru: Две соседки и соседи спорят из-за высоты изгороди, но медиатор помогает им услышать друг друга. За бытовым конфликтом проступает история утраты.
text:
Mr Hargreaves: I want it noted, before we begin, that I have lived at number fourteen for forty-one years, and in that time the hedge has never once been a problem.
Priya: I want it noted that I moved in eight months ago, and the hedge has been a problem since the first morning.
Tom: All right. Thank you both. I'm Tom, I'm a volunteer mediator with the council, and my only job is to make sure each of you is heard. Mr Hargreaves, would you like to start?
Mr Hargreaves: Very well. The hedge is a privet, planted in 1983 by my late wife, and it is three metres tall. Miss Nair has asked me to cut it down to one and a half.

Priya: Two. I asked for two metres. And it's Priya, please.
Mr Hargreaves: Two, then. Which is still an act of butchery.
Tom: Priya, can you tell us why the height matters to you?
Priya: Because it blocks every scrap of light from my kitchen and my vegetable bed. I work from home, and from October to March I'm sitting in what feels like a cupboard. I've bought a daylight lamp. I'm thirty-two, and I'm buying artificial sunshine.

Mr Hargreaves: She bought the house knowing the hedge was there.
Priya: I bought it in July, when the sun was high and the agent talked about "mature planting." Nobody mentioned that it would swallow the garden by Christmas.
Mr Hargreaves: And there is the matter of the birds. A pair of blackbirds has nested in it every spring since before she arrived. One cannot simply hack away a home in March.
Priya: That's fair. I hadn't thought of the birds. We could do the work in winter, before nesting starts.
Mr Hargreaves: Hm. That is, I concede, a reasonable point, which irritates me.

Tom: So there are two things. A hedge that matters to Mr Hargreaves for sentimental reasons, and a loss of light that affects Priya's daily life. Is that fair?
Mr Hargreaves: Sentimental is a word people use when they mean unimportant.
Tom: I don't think I did, and I don't think Priya did either. Mr Hargreaves, what does the hedge mean to you?
Mr Hargreaves: It means that she's still out there, pruning on Sunday mornings, in that terrible straw hat. She planted it for privacy. In the early years we were rather in the public eye, because of my work with the railway, and she wanted a quiet garden.

Priya: I didn't know that. When I first came round, you were so brusque that I assumed you simply disliked the neighbours.
Mr Hargreaves: I dislike surprises, which is a different matter entirely. My wife was the sociable one. After she died, I rather lost the knack.
Priya: I didn't know that either.
Mr Hargreaves: There's no reason you should. Most people on this street have forgotten what I did for a living, and I have never been tempted to remind them. I've trimmed it myself every autumn since she died. The ladder is increasingly difficult, I admit, but I couldn't bear to pay a stranger to do it.

Priya: Is that why it's so overgrown? Because you can't manage the top?
Mr Hargreaves: I would not say overgrown. I would say generous.
Tom: Mr Hargreaves, would you object if someone helped you with the maintenance?
Mr Hargreaves: Depends who. I won't have a lad with a petrol hedge-trimmer making a mess of it.

Priya: What if it was me? I don't mean cutting it down, I mean hand shears, the way she did. I could do the sides and the top, and you could tell me exactly how she'd have done it.
Mr Hargreaves: You'd want to remove a metre.
Priya: I'd want to remove sixty centimetres this winter, and see how the light feels. We could review it in spring. If it still isn't enough, we sit down again, and I won't send any more solicitor's letters.
Mr Hargreaves: Those letters were deeply unpleasant, I must say.

Priya: They were. I was angry. I'm sorry about the letters.
Tom: That sounds like real progress, and I appreciate how difficult it was to say.
Priya: Honestly, I'd rather lose the argument and gain a neighbour. I've been rehearsing furious speeches in the shower for weeks, and they were exhausting.
Mr Hargreaves: As were mine, if it is any consolation. I even wrote one out in fountain pen.

Tom: With that in mind, Mr Hargreaves, how does the proposal strike you?
Mr Hargreaves: With reservations. Sixty centimetres is a considerable loss. But I find, rather unexpectedly, that I do not hate the idea of company on the ladder. I'm seventy-nine, you see, and the ladder has stopped being funny.
Priya: I'll hold it steady, and I promise I won't touch the roses on the fence.
Mr Hargreaves: Those are hers too, though. She planted them in 1991.
Priya: Then I'll treat them like museum pieces. And in return, I'd love to give you tomatoes in August. They'll finally have some sunshine.

Mr Hargreaves: I've never liked tomatoes. The skins are tough and the flavour is overrated.
Priya: You haven't tried mine. I grew them from seed.
Mr Hargreaves: Hm. I shall reserve judgement, as I do with all things that come in a punnet. Though I might make an exception for a very small one.
Tom: Shall I write up the agreement? Sixty centimetres off the top this winter, shared work with hand tools, a review in April, and no more letters from solicitors.

Mr Hargreaves: And the straw hat?
Tom: I'm sorry, the straw hat?
Mr Hargreaves: I should like it recorded that if Miss Nair is going to prune the hedge, she may borrow the hat. It hangs in the shed, and it has been wasted there for years.
Priya: I'd be honoured. Truly.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: ˈmediator, ˈmaintenance, conˈsiderable. В maintenance ударение на первом слоге, а не на «-ten».
Звук «h» лёгкий выдох без трения, как в hedge, hat. Но в honoured «h» не произносится вовсе.
Звук «w»: губы округлены и вытянуты вперёд, как при «у», затем быстро раскрываются; не путайте с «в».
Дифтонг «aʊ»: начинайте с широкого «а» и плавно уходите к «у»: how, house.

questions.question: What is the dispute about?
questions.answer: A three-metre privet hedge that blocks light from Priya's kitchen and garden.

questions.question: Why does Mr Hargreaves care about the hedge?
questions.answer: His late wife planted it, and it reminds him of her.

questions.question: What compromise do they reach?
questions.answer: Priya removes sixty centimetres by hand with his guidance, with a review in spring.

questions.question: What does Mr Hargreaves offer at the end?
questions.answer: He lets Priya borrow his late wife's straw hat.
